newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Black S.African business buoyed by landmark sale.
newsitem.headline: Black S.African business buoyed by landmark sale.

text.p: Anglo American's sale of a chunk of its empire to black businessmen is a success which should open the doors to more deals to boost black economic empowerment in South Africa, analysts said on Thursday.

The National Empowerment Consortium (NEC), housing 50 black economic interest groups, will buy a dominant stake in Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd (Johnnic), which is valued at 4.2 billion rand ($930 million), in a deal announced on Wednesday.
"It is still small compared with white South Africa, but with the first deal under the belt, the next ones should be able to progress more quickly," said economist Tony Twine.
However, no deals on the same scale were in the pipeline.
Shares in New Africa Investments Ltd, one of the NEC's main members, jumped on Thursday on news of the sale.
The price leapt to an intraday high of 290 cents -- up 16 percent from its previous 250 cents close -- before retracing to 274 by early afternoon on profit-taking in brisk trade.
The Johnnic sale is part of a widespread "unbundling" or sell-off of assets by a handful of huge conglomerates who dominate South Africa's gold- and mining-based economy.
"Eighty percent of the JSE must be permanently twitchy because they look like giant nationalisation targets should anyone from the far left sweep to power," Twine said.
That looks unlikely at present.

President Nelson Mandela has ditched the socialist rhetoric of old for market-friendly policies, resisting pressure inside his African National Congress for state action to close the economic gap which could become apartheid's most lasting legacy.
Apart from limited state aid and land reform, blacks will have to rely on their own devices to make economic headway.
Some critics say the NEC is in danger of becoming a black business monolith like its white rivals, enriching its owners but making little difference to ordinary blacks.
But analysts were optimistic the Johnnic deal, clinched after two years of negotiation, could be just the jump-start fledgling black business needed.

The Johnnic sale lifts the market value of companies in which blacks have control or exercise influence to more than 90 billion rand ($20 billion), or about 10 percent of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange's (JSE) market capitalisation.
Johnnic's assets include stakes in South African Breweries, Toyota South Africa and media groups.
"This transaction in many ways deepens and enhances the whole process of black economic empowerment," said chief NEC negotiator, Cyril Ramaphosa.
"It will allow the previously disadvantaged community to play a role they should have played in years past."
Once tipped as President Nelson Mandela's successor, he quit politics this year for business in a symbolic sign of the shift in the fight for black power from politics to the economy.
Whites yielded control of government in 1994 but have ostentatiously clung on to the money and riches of South Africa.
Anglo said late in 1994 it would sell its stake in Johnnic, but only to a group that would further black empowerment.
"The fact that we came out with this conclusion bodes extremely well for...South Africa and its determination to be a winning nation," said Anglo's deputy chairman Nicky Oppenheimer.
The slow march forwards of black business has been marked by involvement in such investment holding companies rather than the creation of much-needed new jobs through manufacturing.
